body_ar: وبهذا تعلمون أن حفص الدوري مثلا توفي في القرن الثالث والخاقاني توفي في القرن الرابع، ومكي بن أبي طالب توفي في القرن الخامس، وأهل الأندلس عموما اشتهروا بإتقان هذا العلم ولذلك فإن مكيا كان مجددا فيه ثم جاء بعده أبو عمرو الداني وهو إمام علوم القرآن كلها بلا منازع، ثم بعده تلميذه أبو داود سليمان بن النجيح وهو كذلك خليفة الداني في هذا العلم، فأهل الأندلس اشتهروا بعلوم التجويد وبتفسير القرآن كذلك فمنهم ابن عطية وابن جزي والقرطبي وأبو بكر بن العربي وغيرهم من أئمة أهل التجويد كأبي حيان وابن الفرس المالكي مؤلف كتاب أحكام القرآن، فلهم مؤلفات كثيرة جدا في خدمة القرآن..
body_en: And by this you know that Hafs al-Duri, for example, died in the third century; that al-Khaqani died in the fourth century; and that Makki ibn Abi Talib died in the fifth century. The people of al-Andalus in general were renowned for their mastery of this science, and for that reason Makki was a renewer in it. Then after him came Abu ʿAmr al-Dani, who is the imam of all the Qur'anic sciences without dispute; then after him his student Abu Dawud Sulayman ibn al-Najih, who is likewise al-Dani's successor in this science. The people of al-Andalus were renowned for the sciences of recitation, and for the exegesis of the Qur'an as well: among them Ibn ʿAtiyyah, Ibn Juzayy, al-Qurtubi and Abu Bakr ibn al-ʿArabi, and others among the leading authorities of the people of tajwīd, such as Abu Hayyan and Ibn al-Faras al-Maliki, the author of the book Aḥkām al-Qurʾān. They have very many works indeed in the service of the Qur'an..

flags.context: the first name in the chronological list
options: Hafs al-Duri [Abu ʿUmar Hafs ibn ʿUmar al-Duri]
flags.note: Serious risk of confusion for an English reader. The Duri meant here is Abu ʿUmar Hafs ibn ʿUmar al-Duri, the transmitter of the readings of Abu ʿAmr and of al-Kisa'i, who did die in the third century. Printed as 'Hafs' alone, the name will be taken for Hafs ibn Sulayman, the transmitter of ʿAsim's reading after whom the standard printed muṣḥaf is named, who is a different man of a different century. Option 0 supplies the full name in brackets. This is an expansion the English reader requires and is recorded rather than made silently.

options: Abu Dawud Sulayman ibn al-Najih [as printed]
Abu Dawud Sulayman ibn Abi al-Qasim Najah
flags.note: PROBABLE SOURCE DEFECT. The scholar described — Abu ʿAmr al-Dani's foremost student and his successor in the Qur'anic sciences in al-Andalus — is known as Sulayman ibn Najah, not ibn al-Najih. The printed form is most likely a transcription slip from the spoken lecture. Translated as printed under the rule against silently repairing the source; a reviewer should settle it against the audio before the name is indexed.

translator_notes: Qur'anic and hadith renderings in this file are interpretive translations of meaning, offered to carry the Sheikh's argument in English. They are not a substitute for the Arabic.
The date shown by the CMS is a bulk-upload timestamp shared by every item in this range, not the date the Sheikh gave the answer. The real date of composition is unknown. See date_is_cms_bulk_upload.

This record belongs to the Sheikh's commentary on the Muqaddimah al-Jazariyyah, Ibn al-Jazari's versified primer on the rules of Qur'anic recitation. The CMS holds the tapes out of order across ids 641–646 and the part numbers in the titles do not run with the ids; the series should be ordered by the number in the title, not by id.

EXCERPT ONLY. The published text breaks off and the full material is offered as a .docx download ('taḥmīl al-māddah'). The English ends exactly where the Arabic ends. The download-link label has been removed from body_ar as a navigation element and recorded in source_download_link.
'A renewer' renders mujaddid, one who revives a discipline in his age; it is a term of art and not a general compliment.
'The leading authorities' renders aʾimmah, the plural of imām in its sense of a recognised authority in a science, not of one who leads prayer.

The list mixes exegetes (Ibn ʿAtiyyah, Ibn Juzayy, al-Qurtubi, Ibn al-ʿArabi) with authorities on recitation, as the Arabic does; the sentence structure has been kept so that the reader can see the Sheikh is naming al-Andalus's contribution to both fields.
Proper names are given in standard romanisation without diacritics in the body, per house style.
